title: The Three Refuges—Coming Home and Living by Vow
speaker: IkuShun Desiree Webster
summary: IkuShun Desiree Webster takes up the three refuges, drawing on Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow, Reb Anderson's Being Upright, and Thich Nhat Hanh's Plum Village verses. IkuShun opens with an image of a traveler closing the door of a hut and lighting a fire against a storm, then recalls Dogen hanging the words Buddha, Dharma and Sangha on his sickroom pillar and circumambulating while chanting the refuges. Taking refuge begins as shelter and coming home, then deepens into vow, as Thay's teaching that the Buddha takes refuge in me makes the practice reciprocal. IkuShun closes on Reb's image of the Buddhas and ancestors saying "Welcome home," then sends everyone into small groups.

sentences.text: He talks about coming in quickly into his little hut, closing the door and lighting a fire, and it didn't take long before the place was nice and cozy and toasty, despite the blustery storm outside.
He enjoyed the very quiet stillness in there.
It was, I think, my first vision of taking refuge in the Buddha and in this way of life, and I still think about it to this day.
So Hannah spoke of repentance last week in Shohaku Okumura's book Living by Vow.
He quotes Banjin Doton, who comments on the precepts.
*We usually think that delusive thoughts and true reality are separate and distinct, as an owner and something that is owned.
When we're completely liberated, we see that there is no person that possesses delusions nor any delusions that are possessed.
This is the true path of the Buddha Dharma.
We should not understand the repentance verse to mean that we first get rid of delusive thoughts by sitting upright and being mindful of the true reality.
Repentance is another name for the three treasures.
To repent is to take refuge in the three treasures.
In the Dharma, repentance is carried out and it completely includes the three treasures and the threefold pure precepts,* which I'm sure we'll talk about soon.
*Repentance, the three refuges and the threefold pure precepts are not apart from falsehood caused by delusions.
We are, however, able to attain liberation within delusions.
We could say that before delusions leave, true reality has arrived.*
And there's a Zen saying that says, before the donkey leaves, the horse has arrived.
That's what it means.
We learn that repentance is nothing other than the Dharma, the practice of Buddha's awakening.
Banjin Doton said that to awaken to the reality that exists prior to separation between delusion and enlightenment, between living beings and Buddhas, is the essence of repentance.
So many of you have heard that our great master Dogen, when he was approaching his death, did not write out one last great speech.
He didn't compose a great death poem.
He didn't go into a deep trance of meditation.
According to Reb Anderson in Being Upright, what he did was take out a long piece of paper and, in great big black letters, write the words Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.
He took that paper and hung it on the pillar in his death bed, ill sick room, and started circumambulating and chanting, "I take refuge in the Buddha.
I take refuge in the Dharma.
I take refuge in the Sangha."
Reb goes on: he brought his whole life energy forward to walk around these three jewels.
He gave his whole life to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha, which means he gave his whole life to all living beings.
Many of you, I'm sure, recall sewing your rakusu or okesa and having Kanho Chris remind you with every stitch, "namu kie butsu, namu kie butsu."
I still remember that.
So our version of taking refuge at Red Cedar is as follows.
*I take refuge in Buddha before all beings, immersing body and mind deeply in the way, awakening true mind.
I take refuge in Dharma before all beings, entering deeply the merciful ocean of Buddha's way.
I take refuge in Sangha before all beings, bringing harmony to everyone, free from hindrance.*
So, excuse me, I found another version of this:
*Taking refuge in the Buddha, we vow with all beings to walk his path of wisdom and compassion.
Taking refuge in the Dharma, we vow to share the teachings of the wisdom as boundless as the ocean.
Taking refuge in Sangha, we vow to create harmony without hindrance.*
So by taking refuge, Shohaku Okumura Roshi says, we make clear the direction that we want to follow.
I like that line.
I can hold the three refuges at different levels.
The first level is the way that I first experienced it: a protection, a place of safety, a coming home.
When I first discovered that I was Buddhist, before I had taken any formal vows, I discovered what it meant to take refuge.
As Thich Nhat Hanh described, I felt the stability of the three treasures somehow.
I discovered that I could always return home in the blink of an eye.
I could recollect how to have the safety, the protection, the fearlessness of returning to this refuge whenever I wanted.
Here I touch the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha as one.
It is for me the true reality which is always shining through, always available to me right now.
I only need to recollect this.
I don't need to go searching for it as if I'm lost in the woods.
I don't need to reestablish a fire in the hearth.
It's already there waiting for me.
As my practice deepened, I also felt that this taking refuge is a vow, not just as words when we're taking our precepts, but as a deep commitment every time we recite them and in every step.
So I wanted to explore it a little bit.
One version of the three refuges from Plum Village is as follows.
*I take refuge in the Buddha, the one who shows me this way in this life.
I take refuge in the Dharma, the way of understanding and love.
I take refuge in the Sangha, the community that lives in harmony and awareness.*

Thich Nhat Hanh says that when we take refuge in the Buddha, we express trust in our capacity to walk in the direction of beauty, truth, and deep understanding, based on our own experience of the efficacy of our practice.
When we take refuge in the Dharma, we enter the path of transformation, the path to end suffering.
When we take refuge in the Sangha, we focus our energies on building our communities that dwell in mindfulness, harmony, and peace.
When we touch these three jewels directly and experience their capacity to bring about transformation and peace, our faith is strengthened even further.
The three jewels are not notions.
They are our life.
*Dwelling in the refuge of Buddha, I clearly see the path of light and beauty in this world.
Dwelling in the refuge of Dharma, I learn to open many doors on the path of transformation.
Dwelling in the refuge of Sangha, I am supported by this shining light that keeps my practice free of obstacles.*
So in the Plum Village tradition of Thich Nhat Hanh, the practitioners always say, "I go back to and rely on the Buddha in myself."
Adding "in myself" makes it clear that we ourselves are Buddha.
When we take refuge in the Buddha, we must always understand that the Buddha takes refuge in me.
Without the second part, Thay says, the first part is not complete.
There's a short verse, a little gatha, that they say:
*I entrust myself to the earth.
The earth entrusts herself to me.
I entrust myself to Buddha.
Buddha entrusts himself or herself to me.*
During the Buddha's last months, he always taught, take refuge in yourself, not in anything else.
In you, the Buddha and Dharma and Sangha are there.
Don't look for things that are far away.
Be an island unto yourself.
When you get lost or confused or angry, if you practice mindful breathing and return to the island of yourself, you will be in a safe place.
Buddha is our mindfulness, Dharma is our conscious breathing, and Sangha is our five aggregates working in harmony.
Another way of looking at this is through Reb Anderson's eyes again, from Being Upright.
To take refuge in Buddha means to take refuge in what you really are.
What you really are is already attained, always, in every moment.
What you really are is Buddha.
Taking refuge in Buddha means trusting that you are Buddha.
*Taking refuge in the Buddha in myself, I aspire to help all people recognize their own awakened nature and realize the mind of love.*
I understand now why this taking the refuges is also taking vow.
It is because at some level, I know that the Buddha is in me.
Taking refuge means not only that I take refuge in Buddha, but that the Buddha takes refuge in me.
It is a commitment.
It is a vow, every time I take refuge.
*Taking refuge in the Dharma in myself, I aspire to help all people grasp the practice and walk together on the path of liberation.*
Thay says, Dharma books and studies are valuable, but the true Dharma is revealed from our life and our practice.
Whenever the Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path are practiced, the living Dharma is there.
There are 84,000 Dharma doors.
Sitting meditation is one door.
Walking meditation is another door.
To take refuge in the Dharma is to choose the doors that are most appropriate for us.
Dharma is great compassion, understanding, and love.
To realize these qualities, we need a sangha.
*Taking refuge in the Sangha in myself, I aspire to help all people build communities and encourage the transformation of all beings.*
Sangha is the community of practitioners as well as other elements that support our practice: our cushion, our walking path, the trees, the sky, and other living beings.
I keep getting this little strange thing here.
Thay says that in his country there is a saying that when the tiger leaves the mountains and goes to the lowlands, he will be caught by humans and killed.
When a practitioner leaves her sangha, she may abandon her practice and even die as a practitioner.
Practicing with sangha is essential.
Even if we have a deep appreciation for the practice, it can be difficult to continue without the support of friends.
We have individual eyes and we have sangha eyes.
When a sangha shines its light on our personal views, we see more clearly.
This of course includes teachers.
They can often see more clearly places where I don't see, either because they are hidden from me or because I refuse to acknowledge them because of my ego mind directing me to avoid them.
With my teacher's skill, I can uncover some of the hindrances that have clouded my view for much of this life.
I also rely on our community to keep my aspiration alive, and I look to the sangha, individuals, and community for inspiration.
People in our community model the way of practicing in the world.
They do inspire me.
I only need to glance at another during our zazen and see how beautifully they are sitting, upright and with great strength, to realize my own commitment and my vow.
So taking refuge in this way, recognizing that it is a reciprocal taking refuge, reinforces the understanding of interdependence.
It opens us up to all the precepts.
Taking refuge for me started out as a place of shelter, for safety, for fearlessness.

As I practiced, I started feeling that this was a place of commitment, a place of living by vow, and this way of understanding that it is a mutual exchange, not a one-way direction, really helps me to see this.
As Reb says, when you take refuge and you give your devotion to the Buddha way, there is always a response.
All the Buddhas and ancestors say, "Welcome home.
Glad to see you.
We've been waiting."
And we see that it's a concert, not a solo performance.
That's what Reb says.
These feelings are reflected every time I think of the act of taking refuge in the Buddha and the Buddha taking refuge in me.
*In the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, in myself, I vow to hold this place of refuge with reverence, understanding, and love.*
So that's my little take on the Three Jewels.
Thank you very much.
Of course, now I would like to have everybody get into groups for a little bit.
Maybe we can get in.
